findings.title: The Upstash client has NO timeout and a 3s blocking sleep-retry, so a slow/hung Upstash never raises: every fail-open except block is unreachable and the single event loop stalls forever
findings.dedupe: new
findings.fix: At client construction in cache_service.py, replace the SDK's default transport with a bounded one and disable the sleep-retry: `redis_client = Redis(url=..., token=..., rest_retries=0)` then `redis_client._http._client = httpx.Client(timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=1.0, read=2.0, write=2.0, pool=1.0))`. Gate the whole thing behind a new default-ON-after-canary flag ENABLE_UPSTASH_TIMEOUT (read per call at init only, so a bad value can be reverted by redeploy) and log the effective timeout once at startup like the serper gate does. With a real timeout the existing `except Exception -> fail-open` blocks finally do what their docstrings claim. Do this BEFORE flipping ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD, or a hang just moves into the 40-thread executor and exhausts it instead.

Second red test: monkeypatch cache_service.redis_client with a fake whose .get() sleeps 5s, run `asyncio.wait_for(auth_service._is_token_revoked_async(tok), timeout=3)` and assert it raises TimeoutError today (proving no internal deadline) and returns False (fail-open) after the fix.
findings.impact: Every Redis-dependent handler (cache read, freemium gate, budget gate, token revocation) calls a BLOCKING httpx POST with no deadline on the single uvicorn worker's event loop (ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD is absent from all 54 Railway `web` vars, so the #115 offload dispatches are inert). During an Upstash slowdown/partition the process does not fail open -- it fails HANG: the whole deployment (1 replica x 1 worker) stops answering /health, /auth/me, /usage/status and every compare, and Railway's ON_FAILURE restart budget (max 3) is the only recovery. On a connection ERROR the SDK sleeps 3s synchronously then retries once, so a cold compare's ~30-70 commands become up to 90-210s of event-loop freeze inside a 30s STREAM_HARD_CAP. This is the root reason the M18 'everything fails open' thesis is wrong in the worst case.

If/when a second worker lands, upgrade to a Redis reservation key (`SET lock:{cache_key} <id> NX EX 45`) with the loser polling the value key -- but do NOT do that before LS-CACHE-REDIS-01, or the lock itself can hang.

findings.impact: The whole cache-hit-rate story assumes the first requester warms the key before the second arrives. It does not: the resolve window is ~30s (search_logs SUCCESS-ONLY p90=18.5s, p95=23.8s, p99=30.0s), and every request that lands inside it pays the FULL cold cost again -- OpenAI parse+specs+reviews+verdict and the Serper/Firecrawl/Scrape.do fan-out. At the M18 ceiling of ~10 compares/min deployment-wide, a single trending pair (a push notification, a TikTok, a launch tweet) converts the entire per-minute budget into N duplicate pipelines for ONE product pair: 10 requests on the same pair = 10x OpenAI tokens, 10x Serper credits, 10x scrape spend, and 10x the 40-thread executor pressure, for one cacheable answer. It also breaks the freemium economics: those 10 duplicate compares each burn a paid credit AND a user credit.

findings.title: Logout never revokes the Supabase session: sign_out() is called on a fresh session-less anon client, so the ONLY revocation is a 1-hour Redis key that fails open
findings.dedupe: new
findings.fix: Revoke server-side, not just in Redis. In logout_user, build a user-scoped client and sign out the actual session: `client = create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_ANON_KEY); client.auth.set_session(access_token, refresh_token); client.auth.sign_out(scope='global')` -- which requires the mobile client to POST the refresh_token to /auth/logout (add it to the request body; it is already in the device's SecureStore). Keep the Redis blacklist as the fast local check but stop treating it as the revocation mechanism, and make the route return 502 (not success:true) when the Supabase sign-out call fails, so the app can retry. Ship the body change behind a tolerant server (refresh_token optional) so the OTA gap does not break existing clients.
findings.test_first: tests/test_logout_revokes_session.py: TestClient POST /auth/v1/logout with a stubbed auth client; assert the stub recorded a set_session(access_token, refresh_token) followed by sign_out(scope='global'). Second red test: with cache_service.redis_client = None, assert POST /auth/logout returns a non-200 (or at least that a subsequent /auth/me with the same token is rejected). Both red today.
findings.impact: A user who taps Log out, or an admin responding to a stolen-device report, gets no server-side revocation. The refresh token stays valid, so anyone holding the captured token pair can mint fresh access tokens indefinitely. Even the 1-hour access-token blacklist evaporates the moment Upstash is unreachable or the key TTL passes. Combined with MB-security-06 (Google sign-in has no nonce binding), the app has no working session-invalidation primitive at all -- which is a launch blocker for an app that stores purchase history and referral balances.

verdict_trail.reason: Stronger than the finder claimed. I read the installed gotrue sign_out: it does `session = self.get_session(); access_token = session.access_token if session else None; if access_token: self.admin.sign_out(...)`. A client from create_client() has empty per-client memory storage, so access_token is None and the revoke call is never issued — a mechanism proof, not an inference. Route is live and any exception still returns success:true. Only real revocation is a 1h Redis key with fail-open reads. Not in M13/M18 (grepped). Corrected line 288 (blank) to 290. Local supabase_auth is off-lock (2.28.0 vs 2.31.0); the get_session gate is stable across versions.

Stronger than a reading. I ran the real logout_user with a genuine anon client whose gotrue `_request` and `admin.sign_out` were instrumented: ZERO HTTP requests issued, admin.sign_out never called, route contract returns success:true, and the only artefact is a 1 h `revoked:<sha256>` key; with redis_client None or raising, _is_token_revoked returns False (fail-open, unlogged). The mechanism holds at the PINNED supabase-auth 2.31.0, which the first verifier did not check: sign_out calls admin.sign_out only when get_session() yields a token, and a fresh create_client has empty storage. The proposed fix closes it but is heavier than needed — admin.sign_out(jwt,'global') POSTs /logout with the access token alone, so no refresh_token body change or OTA is required. test_first pins the proposed implementation; assert the /logout POST instead.

findings.title: All 9 Redis-backed gates fail open simultaneously and every one is inline-blocking in prod: an Upstash outage removes the freemium cap, all spend gates, the model cap, token revocation and brute-force lockout at the exact moment cost amplifies
findings.dedupe: known:M13-36 + M18 LS-event-loop-04/05 narrative — still-open (no logging added at HEAD; ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD still unset in prod)
findings.fix: Two changes, both small. (a) Observability: add `logger.warning` + `sentry_service.capture_message` to all 9 handlers (behaviour unchanged) so an operator can see the cascade; today it is silent. (b) Asymmetric policy: keep fail-OPEN for availability gates (freemium, revocation, lockout are the M13-36 call) but flip the SPEND gates to fail-CLOSED-after-N-consecutive-errors -- a module-level consecutive-error counter in api_budget_service that, once >= 5, makes has_budget/is_circuit_closed return False until one succeeds. Ship behind ENABLE_SPEND_GATE_FAIL_CLOSED (default OFF) and canary it only after LS-CACHE-REDIS-01 gives Redis a real timeout, because without a timeout the errors never arrive as errors.
findings.test_first: tests/test_redis_outage_cascade.py: parametrize over the 9 gate entry points with cache_service.redis_client swapped for a fake whose every method raises ConnectionError; assert each returns its permissive value AND that a warning was logged (caplog) and sentry_service.capture_message was called. The log/Sentry half is red today for all 9.
findings.impact: During an Upstash incident the system simultaneously: serves every request as a full COLD pipeline (no cache), grants unlimited free comparisons (TIER_LIMITS 3/day + 10/month unenforced), grants unlimited Firecrawl/Scrape.do/Serper/Brightdata spend (has_budget True, breakers closed), routes every verdict to the expensive model (usage reads 0), accepts revoked tokens, and disables login lockout. The spend meters die exactly when spend amplifies -- an outage is the single most expensive minute the system can have, and it is also the least protected. M13-36 (P2, auth's three controls fail open with zero observability) and the M18 narrative note are STILL OPEN at HEAD: `_is_token_revoked` and `check_account_locked` still have bare `except: return False` with no logger and no Sentry.

verdict_trail.reason: The enumeration is real — I opened all 9 sites and every one fails open, and ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD is absent from the 54 web vars so all run inline. But the finding's actionable delta is falsified: it claims all 9 are silent and that the log/Sentry test is red for all 9. Seven of nine already log a warning (usage_service:280, api_budget:248/391/562, serper_service:276, model_router:92), and gates using _redis_get/_redis_incr also log at ERROR in cache_service:63/89. The only two silent gates are auth_service:317 and :574 — exactly M13-36. Gate 2 is also unreachable (ENABLE_ANON_USAGE_GATE unset, #128). Residual over prior reviews is a design proposal, not a new defect.

findings.title: The nogenuine sentinel caches an ESTIMATED/CONVERTED price object for 30 days -- 30x the 24h TTL the identical object gets in the positive cache -- and the invalidation fix for it ships dark
findings.dedupe: known:#53 — still-open (fix shipped dark, ENABLE_NEGCACHE_GENUINE_INVALIDATION absent from Railway web); the 30x TTL inversion itself is new
findings.fix: Split the sentinel from the payload. Store `{'_dead_end': True, 'checked_at': ts}` under `nogenuine:{key}` for the 30d structural TTL (that fact IS stable), and keep the actual price under the normal price key at price_cache_ttl(price) = 24h. On a sentinel hit with no live price key, skip the Tier-1.5 cascade but re-resolve the cheap tiers so the served number is at most a day old. No new flag is needed for the split (it strictly shortens a price's life); DO flip ENABLE_NEGCACHE_GENUINE_INVALIDATION on in the same canary so a later genuine resolution clears the sentinel (#53).
findings.test_first: tests/test_negcache_ttl_policy.py: patch scs.set_negative_cache and scs.set_cached with recorders, drive the negative-cache write helper with an estimated price -> assert the PRICE object was written with ttl == PRICE_CACHE_TTL (86400) and that the 30-day write contains no 'amount' key. Red today (amount is present at ttl 2592000).
findings.impact: For every product where the cascade once failed to find a genuine BH source -- by design the luxury fragrance / haircare / gadget categories that are the app's core catalogue -- users are shown a price that can be 30 days stale, while a genuine price for the same product would have been refreshed after 7 days and a converted one after 24 hours. The cache POLICY says a price we cannot vouch for should refresh sooner (price_service.py:159-165 says exactly that); the negative cache does the opposite. #53 already documents the never-deleted half; this is the TTL-inversion half, and the mitigation for both is dark in prod.

verdict_trail.reason: TTL inversion confirmed: the sentinel stores the price object itself at 2,592,000s while price_cache_ttl() would give that same estimate 86,400s (30x, arithmetic recomputed from the constants) and the read serves it back verbatim. One evidence error corrected: the finder says the #53 fix exists at HEAD as _negcache_genuine_invalidation_enabled() shipping dark. `git grep ENABLE_NEGCACHE_GENUINE_INVALIDATION 76ace90 -- app/` returns nothing — that helper lands in commit 98231bd, five commits AFTER the review SHA; the finder read a drifted working tree. #53 is still-open because it is unimplemented at HEAD, not because a flag is off. Two narrowings: converted_usd and validation_rejected are excluded by should_negative_cache.

findings.title: Dashboard counters are 43% of the warm per-product Upstash budget and every one costs two commands because EXPIRE is a separate non-atomic call after INCR
findings.dedupe: new
findings.fix: Replace `INCR then conditional EXPIRE` with a single command that always carries the TTL. Upstash REST supports SET with EX and GETSET semantics, but the cheapest correct form here is a pipeline: `redis_client.pipeline()` (upstash-redis 1.7.0 exposes it) issuing INCR+EXPIRE as ONE HTTP round trip -- that halves the round trips and makes the TTL unconditional, killing the leak. Add a `_incr_with_ttl(key, ttl)` helper in cache_service and convert all 7 call sites mechanically. Separately, batch the per-product metric writes into one pipeline at the end of _fetch_product_data (they are already fire-and-forget), taking the warm side from 14 to ~8 commands.
findings.test_first: tests/test_metric_counter_atomic_ttl.py: counting fake Redis, call cache_service.record_price_outcome twice for the same category/day, assert exactly ONE round trip per call and that the key's TTL is set on BOTH calls (today the second call sets no TTL, and a fake whose expire() raises leaves the key immortal). Red today.
findings.impact: Upstash bills per command, so the /admin/costs dashboard counters cost as much per warm compare as the actual product cache does (6 vs 5 commands per side), and each is a blocking round trip on the loop. At 10,000 DAU x 1 compare/day that is ~120k purely-observational commands/day. The non-atomicity is also a storage leak: if the process dies or Redis errors between the INCR that returned 1 and the EXPIRE, the key gets NO TTL and lives forever in Upstash (which bills storage) -- and there is no sweeper.

verdict_trail.reason: Reproduced. I re-ran the warm harness against the real _fetch_product_data: total_commands=14, same 6 metric commands (6/14=43%). All five INCR/EXPIRE pairs exist and none has an offload dispatch; all seven scs.py call sites are exactly as cited. Non-atomic TTL leak is real (EXPIRE only fires when INCR==1). Fix is feasible: requirements.txt pins upstash-redis==1.7.0 and Redis exposes pipeline/multi. Two nits: cache_obs pair is at 350-351 not 351-353, and the event-loop half overlaps M13-06.

findings.dedupe: known:M13-49 — still-open at HEAD; new evidence = all three knobs are actually SET on both Railway services

Then REMOVE MAX_MONTHLY_COST, FREE_TIER_DAILY_LIMIT and CACHE_DURATION from both Railway services so no operator reads them as live controls, and if a real monthly ceiling is wanted, implement it in api_budget_service where the meters actually live. findings.test_first: tests/test_no_orphan_cache_api.py: assert that each of the 12 names is absent from cache_service's module namespace (i.e. deleted), and a companion assert that `os.getenv('MAX_MONTHLY_COST')` appears nowhere under app/. Red today.

FREE_TIER_DAILY_LIMIT being set implies the operator believes the free daily cap is tunable; it is 3, hardcoded, and the orphan block would grant 5 (a 67% overrun) if anything ever wired it. verdict_trail.reason: Confirmed and correctly flagged as known. My own word-boundary scan over app/+scripts/+tests/ (excluding cache_service.py) returns 0 for all 12 names; get_cached_price was rightly excluded (8 hits, but that is product_data_service's async shadow). findings.title: There is no comparison-level result cache at all: the shipped get_comparison_cache/set_comparison_cache have zero callers, so an identical repeat compare re-pays the verdict LLM even when every sub-cache is warm
findings.dedupe: new (M13-49 flags the orphan block as dead code; the missing result-cache layer and its measured repeat-rate consequence are not in any prior review)
findings.fix: Cache the assembled comparison response under `comparison:{region}:{sorted product pair}:{schema_version}` with a SHORT TTL (30-60 min -- long enough to absorb the repeat head, short enough that a price refresh is visible) and serve it with an explicit `_cached: true` + `data_freshness` notice so the UI can label it, reusing attach_data_freshness_notice. Key MUST include the region, the personalization cohort (ENABLE_COHORT_PERSONALIZATION is ON in prod, so verdicts are user-shaped) and a schema version, or you will serve one user's personalized verdict to another -- that is the reason to ship it behind ENABLE_COMPARISON_RESULT_CACHE (default OFF) and canary with cohort personalization forced off first. Do NOT reuse the existing orphan helpers as-is: their key has no region-correct normalization, no cohort axis and no version.
findings.test_first: tests/test_comparison_result_cache.py: with the flag ON, run the same compare twice through the route with all sub-caches warm and extract_specs/generate_comparison patched as counters; assert the verdict counter == 1 and that the second response carries _cached=true. Red today (== 2). A second test must assert that two DIFFERENT cohort ids produce two different cache keys.
findings.impact: Even in the best case where specs, reviews and price are all L1 hits, a repeat of the same pair still runs the extraction + scoring + verdict OpenAI calls and the fact-check pass -- the dominant per-compare cost (M18/M13 both put LLM at ~75% of per-compare spend). With the two most-repeated real pairs in the corpus ('iphone 15 vs galaxy s24' 6,700 times, 'carrier 1.5t ac vs lg 1.5t ac' 1,537) the head of the query distribution is extremely cacheable and nothing caches it. Combined with LS-CACHE-REDIS-02 (no singleflight) the system has neither a temporal nor a concurrent dedupe layer for its most expensive unit of work.

verdict_trail.reason: Structural claim holds. get_comparison_cache_key/get_comparison_cache/set_comparison_cache are at 602/649/655 with 0 callers in my independent scan, and cache_service.py:605 is the only 'comparison:' key anywhere in app/. text_routes.py has no result-level read on the compare path (only the admin flush at :956). ENABLE_COHORT_PERSONALIZATION=true in prod, so the cohort-axis warning in the fix is correct and load-bearing. Measured repeat rates reproduce from dupes.txt and the SELECT-only script; the 7-distinct-user/load-traffic caveat is disclosed. Minor overstatement: with specs warm, extraction is skipped; the verdict LLM is what is re-paid.

findings.title: Upstash RTT from Railway is still unmeasured, so every capacity number in M18 rests on a dev-box 163ms figure that a production code comment presents as authoritative
findings.dedupe: known:M18 LS-capacity-math-02 — still-open (never measured); new = the exact read-only procedure and the observation that the shipped code comment still presents the dev-box number as authoritative
findings.fix:
Run the procedure below ONCE and replace the 163ms literal in serper_service.py:229 with the measured p50/p95 and the date, so no future reader inherits a dev-box number. READ-ONLY PROCEDURE (40 Upstash commands total, all reads/PING, no writes): (1) `railway link` to the project, then `railway ssh --service web --environment production` -- this MUST be `ssh`, not `railway run`, because `railway run` executes on your laptop with prod env vars and measures YOUR network, not the container's. (2) Inside the container run:  python - <<'PY'
import os,time,statistics,urllib.request
url=os.environ['UPSTASH_REDIS_URL'].rstrip('/')+'/ping'
h={'Authorization':'Bearer '+os.environ['UPSTASH_REDIS_TOKEN']}
raw=[]
for _ in range(20):
    t=time.perf_counter(); urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url,headers=h),timeout=10).read(); raw.append((time.perf_counter()-t)*1000); time.sleep(0.2)
raw.sort(); n=len(raw)
print('RAW  n=%d min=%.1f p50=%.1f p90=%.1f p95=%.1f max=%.1f ms'%(n,raw[0],raw[n//2],raw[int(n*0.9)],raw[int(n*0.95)],raw[-1]))
from upstash_redis import Redis
r=Redis(url=os.environ['UPSTASH_REDIS_URL'],token=os.environ['UPSTASH_REDIS_TOKEN'])
sdk=[]
for _ in range(20):
    t=time.perf_counter(); r.get('__m22_rtt_probe_absent_key__'); sdk.append((time.perf_counter()-t)*1000); time.sleep(0.2)
sdk.sort(); n=len(sdk)
print('SDK  n=%d min=%.1f p50=%.1f p90=%.1f p95=%.1f max=%.1f ms'%(n,sdk[0],sdk[n//2],sdk[int(n*0.9)],sdk[int(n*0.95)],sdk[-1]))
PY  (3) Report BOTH numbers: RAW is the network floor, SDK includes base64 encoding, the Upstash-Sync-Token read-your-writes handshake and httpx overhead -- SDK is the one that multiplies the command counts. The GET targets a key that does not exist, so nothing is written and nothing is evicted.
findings.test_first: Not a code defect -- the 'red test' is a docs/CI assertion: add a check that serper_service.py:229 and docs/investigations/*.md do not contain the string '163ms' without an accompanying 'dev-box' qualifier, so the number cannot be re-laundered as production truth before it is measured.
findings.impact: Every load conclusion the campaign has shipped -- '~10 compares/min deployment-wide', 'flags-off blocking bounds the service at 0.15-0.5 cold compares/s', 'the offload waves are worth flipping' -- is linear in this constant. Railway (us-west/Metal) to an Upstash region that may or may not be co-located can plausibly be anywhere from ~5ms (same region) to ~250ms (cross-continent). At 5ms the entire ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD programme is not worth its risk; at 250ms the warm compare alone spends ~9s of pure event-loop stall (36 commands) and the capacity answer is 4x worse than published. Nobody can rank the fix backlog until this is one number.

verdict_trail.reason: Line 229 is exact and the underlying gap is real and still-open, but the one NEW claim is refuted by the text itself: the comment reads 'measured 163ms in this worktree', which IS a dev-box qualifier, not an authoritative production figure. The M18 doc at :110 already states the same caveat, and LS-capacity-math-02 already owns the gap. What remains is a known measurement gap plus a procedure the lane could not run (HARD RULE 1 forbids prod writes / railway ssh). No code defect, no live harm: P3, not P2.

findings.title: Command budget and key cardinality per request type, measured through the real runtime (reference finding, no defect)
findings.dedupe: new
findings.fix: No fix -- this is the measurement the lane was asked to produce, recorded so the other lanes and the capacity model stop guessing. The actionable consequences are filed as LS-CACHE-REDIS-04 (4 wasted commands/compare), -07 (6 metric commands/side, halvable by pipelining), -02 and -10 (the duplicate-work multipliers that make the per-compare number happen N times), and -11 (the RTT the counts must be multiplied by).
findings.test_first: tests/test_redis_command_budget.py as a RATCHET: counting fake Redis, drive a warm _fetch_product_data and assert total commands <= 14 today (tightening to <= 8 after -04 and -07 land), and drive consume_comparison_credit and assert <= 4. Any future change that adds a Redis round trip to the hot path then fails CI instead of arriving silently.
findings.impact: CARDINALITY (modelled from the measured per-compare key writes: up to 10 new keys per DISTINCT compare = 2 specs + 2 reviews + 2 price + up to 2 nogenuine + up to 2 varhint, plus 2 per user per day for usage and 5 per active user for the home/profile view caches). At 100 users x 3 compares/day: ~3,000 key-writes/day, steady state under the 7d TTL ~a few tens of thousands of keys -- comfortably inside Upstash's free tier on storage but ~150k commands/month (free tier is 500K/month), so the free plan survives to roughly 250-350 DAU and no further. At 1,000 users: ~30k key-writes/day, ~1.5M commands/month. At 10,000 users: ~300k key-writes/day, up to ~2.1M live keys at steady state under the 7d product TTLs, and ~15-20M commands/month. The dominant lever is NOT user count but distinct-product count, because the 6 product keys per compare are the only unbounded family; every other family (tier15, price_outcome, cache_obs, budget, circuit, openai:4o) is bounded by category x day or provider and contributes under 5,000 keys total.

verdict_trail.reason: The measured table reproduces: I re-ran the warm harness (14 commands, identical sequence) and confirmed /usage/status, freemium gate 4/3/4, anon 4, provider gate 2, model_router 3, cold price 21, and /admin/costs 5 MGETs = 126+126+21+2226+210 = 2709 exactly. Key-cardinality arithmetic checks (318x7=2226; 30k x 7d = 2.1M keys). BUT the modelled commands/month is ~2x understated by its own inputs: 100 users x 3 compares = 300 compares/day x 36 = ~324k/month, not ~150k; 1,000 users = ~3.2M not 1.5M; 10,000 = ~32M not 15-20M. Free-tier ceiling is nearer 150 DAU at 3 compares/day.

findings.title: P3 sweep: six smaller cache/Redis defects (TTL-less health key, non-atomic TTL leak, dead serper breaker, colliding usage: namespace, sync sitemap probes on the price path, read-your-writes overhead)
findings.dedupe: new (item (b) overlaps the M13-36 incr/expire observation, which was scoped to the auth lockout counter only)
findings.fix: (a) delete cache_service.health_check along with the LS-CACHE-REDIS-09 orphan block. (b) fold into the LS-CACHE-REDIS-07 pipeline fix, which makes the TTL unconditional. (c) either set ENABLE_SERPER_BREAKER=true on Railway `web` (it is memoised, so it costs one extra GET per 60s window -- cheap) or delete the dead breaker path; do not leave it in the third state. (d) rename the orphan family or delete it with the -09 block. (e) hoist the sitemap META probes into the existing _cache_get_async dispatch, or better, batch them into one MGET in sitemap_discovery_service. (f) pass read_your_writes=False on the two read-only code paths, or leave it and just measure the cost once -11's procedure runs.
findings.test_first: One test per item, all red today: (a) assert 'health_check' is absent from cache_service's namespace; (b) counting fake whose expire() raises -> assert record_price_outcome still leaves a TTL (pipeline form); (c) assert ENABLE_SERPER_BREAKER is either in the deployed var set or the breaker symbols are gone (a config-parity test over baseline/railway-web-vars.txt); (d) assert no two key builders in app/ share a first path segment with different semantics; (e) counting fake -> assert sitemap_domains_now_built issues at most ONE round trip regardless of domain count; (f) assert the client is constructed with an explicit read_your_writes value rather than the SDK default.
findings.impact: Individually small: (a) one immortal key if ever wired plus ~25 dead lines; (b) an unbounded slow storage leak proportional to Redis error rate; (c) the highest-volume paid provider has a circuit breaker that exists in code and does nothing in production, so a Serper 403/timeout storm still dispatches every entry point at full timeout on every compare -- the exact failure the M13-32 work was written to stop; (d) an operator flushing `usage:*` would hit both families and an operator flushing only one would think they had reset a user; (e) up to 4 extra blocking round trips per compare in fragrances/makeup/skincare/haircare; (f) a per-command latency tax on a client whose latency has never been measured (LS-CACHE-REDIS-11).

verdict_trail.reason: All six sub-claims reproduce at 76ace90 (worktree is 5 commits ahead; I read via `git show 76ace90:`). Two corrections. (c) is NOT new: M13-32 ("Serper... has metering but no circuit breaker", P2) is the row whose fix shipped as this default-OFF flag — report as known:M13-32 still-open, and its impact is overstated because ENABLE_SERPER_FAIL_FAST=true IS set in prod (timeout cap + key rotate), so a 403/timeout storm does not run "full timeout on every compare". (e) is real but marginal: ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD is also absent from prod vars, so every price-path GET already blocks. P3 bundle rating stands; fixes are flag-safe.

findings.title: HTML price extraction runs ON the event loop, not in the 40-thread pool: measured 270-530 ms per typical cached page and 10.4 s for the largest — the real throughput ceiling, and M18 mis-diagnosed it as a GIL convoy inside the threads
findings.dedupe: known:M18 LS-capacity-math-05 — still-open AND mis-diagnosed: that P3 row says '40 threads parsing up-to-3MB pages contend with the event loop for one GIL'. The parses are not in the threads at all, there is no 3 MB cap on this path, and the correct severity is P1 because it is a direct serial ceiling, not GIL contention.
findings.fix: Move the parse into the executor at the four sites: change the calls to `await asyncio.to_thread(extract_price_from_html, html, product_name, currency, domain, url, **kwargs)` at price_service.py:14090 and price_service.py:15425, and structured_comparison_service.py:1643/:1722. `extract_price_from_html` is already pure-sync with no loop/Redis access on the hot branches, so this is mechanically safe; the only care needed is that it currently reaches `content_safety_service` and `exchange_rate_service` — audit those for awaits before the move (they are sync helpers today). Ship it behind ENABLE_PARSE_OFFLOAD (default OFF) so flag-OFF is byte-identical, and canary it TOGETHER with finding 02's executor resize, because moving 18 parses into a pool that is already oversubscribed by one compare just relocates the queue. Independently and cheaply: add a max_bytes cap to `curl_fetch_html` (price_service.py:13948) mirroring `curl_fetch_html_same_site`'s 3_000_000, which alone removes the 10.4 s tail.
findings.test_first: tests/test_parse_offload.py::test_extract_price_from_html_does_not_block_the_loop — start a 50 ms `asyncio.sleep` heartbeat task, concurrently drive `fetch_page_price` against a monkeypatched `curl_fetch_html` returning the 10 MB corpus page, and assert the heartbeat's max inter-tick gap stays under 200 ms. Red today (the gap is ~10 s), green after the offload.
findings.impact: Single uvicorn worker, single loop. One 18-wide curl fan-out serialises ~18 x ~430 ms = ~7.7 s of hard loop block per cold compare (MODELLED from the measured per-page number), which alone caps the deployment at ~7.8 compares/min — tighter than the 10/min limiter bucket and comparable to the OpenAI wall in finding 06. During each parse EVERY other concurrent request is frozen: /health, SSE heartbeats, auth. A single 10 MB PDP (present in the corpus at max) freezes the entire deployment for 10.4 s, which alone blows the 15 s _PRICE_RACE_TIMEOUT and eats a third of the 30 s prod STREAM_HARD_CAP for every concurrent user. At C=3 concurrent cold compares the loop is ~23 s behind; at C=10 the p95 is dominated entirely by queueing, not by upstream latency.

verdict_trail.reason: Code confirmed at 76ace90: `def extract_price_from_html` (sync) at 12987, called bare from `async def fetch_page_price` (14060) at 14090; to_thread wraps only curl_requests.get. Same shape at scs 1643/1722 and price_service 15425. Reproduced the timing on the real function over _proof (n=1235). M18 LS-capacity-math-05 (P3) is factually wrong ('inside executor threads') — still-open, correctly upgraded. Caveat: fetch_page_price fetches via curl_fetch_html_same_site whose max_bytes=3_000_000 (13988) makes the 10 s tail unreachable there; it survives only on the uncapped curl_fetch_html (scs 2553/2886→2879) and firecrawl/scrapedo. Per-compare 7.7 s is modelled.

CONFIRMED by execution, not reading. I tried to break it three ways and it survived all three; only two sub-claims in the finder's evidence needed correction (both non-load-bearing).

WHAT I RAN (scratchpad C:\Users\SYNACK~1\...\m22-review\verify2\repro.py and fixcheck.py, zero network, repo cwd, HEAD 7dd04c1 with 76ace90 verified as ancestor and lines 12987/13943/13948/14060/14090 IDENTICAL at both SHAs via `git show 76ace90:app/services/price_service.py | grep -n`): (A) size-stratified timing of the REAL `extract_price_from_html` over the real `_proof` corpus (n=1235 files); (B) the loop-blocking test the finder only modelled — a 50 ms `asyncio.sleep` heartbeat task running concurrently with the REAL `await fetch_page_price(...)`, `ps.curl_fetch_html_same_site` monkeypatched to return a corpus page, measuring max inter-tick gap; (C) the finder's proposed fix applied in the harness.

STRUCTURE HOLDS: `def extract_price_from_html(` at :12987 is plain sync; `async def fetch_page_price(` at :14060 calls it BARE at :14090; the only `asyncio.to_thread` in that path (:14025) wraps `curl_requests.get` alone. Live in prod: `ENABLE_PAGE_SCRAPE` defaults true (price_service.py:41) AND is `ENABLE_PAGE_SCRAPE=true` in the Railway `web` vars baseline. Reached via `_curl_scraper` (structured_comparison_service.py:1557) inside `fan_out_price_lookup` (price_service.py:15841), which is unbounded — `tasks = [asyncio.create_task(s(product)) for s in scrapers]`, no semaphore — so every scraper's parse serialises onto the one loop.

TWO CORRECTIONS to the finder's evidence, neither refuting: (1) `fetch_page_price` does NOT call `curl_fetch_html` — it calls `curl_fetch_html_same_site` (:14084), which already truncates `text[:max_bytes]` at 3_000_000 (:14048). So the "10 MB PDP freezes the deployment for 10.4 s" is NOT reachable through :14090; the realistic worst case on that path is a 3 MB body = 2.1 s measured. The uncapped exposure is real but lives at `_fetch_page_price` (structured_comparison_service.py:2877-2879) and :2553, which use the capless `curl_fetch_html` — I measured 7.68 s of loop freeze on the uncapped 9.99 MB corpus page there. Net: same defect, wrong line attributed for the tail; the finder's own proposed cap on `curl_fetch_html` happens to fix the right site. (2) The finder's per-page numbers are non-monotone in size (p50 428.9 ms > p90 269.6 ms), which looked like a measurement artifact; it is not — I reproduce the same inversion (p50 368 KB = 308.5 ms, p90 1684 KB = 206.9 ms) because the JSON-LD rung short-circuits before the full soup on some large pages. Direction and magnitude confirmed.

DOES THE PROPOSED FIX CLOSE MY REPRO? YES. Wrapping the parse in `await asyncio.to_thread(extract_price_from_html, ...)` drops the max heartbeat gap from 320-1250 ms to 79-103 ms on the p50 page, and from 2063-2125 ms to 138-174 ms on the 3 MB body (warm executor, 3 reps each). One caveat I measured and the finder did not: with a COLD default executor the first `to_thread` still costs ~821 ms of gap (thread spin-up), so the fix needs a warmed pool or the first request post-deploy still stalls. And the finder's own warning is validated in reverse — my numbers are single-parse; with N concurrent parses in the pool the GIL convoy M18 hypothesised becomes real only AFTER this offload, so the "canary together with finding 02's executor resize" instruction is correct, not defensive padding.

IS test_first THE RIGHT RED TEST? NO — it is wrong on two counts and would ship green-that-means-nothing. (a) It monkeypatches `curl_fetch_html`, which `fetch_page_price` never calls at HEAD; the patch would not intercept, the real `curl_fetch_html_same_site` would attempt a live network call to the fake URL, return None, and the assertion would pass vacuously against an unexercised parse. Patch `curl_fetch_html_same_site` instead (or split the test: `fetch_page_price` for the 3 MB path, `StructuredComparisonService._fetch_page_price` for the uncapped path). (b) The "10 MB corpus page" premise is unreachable through `fetch_page_price` because of the 3 MB truncation — with the patch point corrected the body under test is 3 MB, which is still red today at ~2.1 s so the <200 ms assertion survives, but for a different reason than stated. Add a `await asyncio.to_thread(lambda: None)` executor warm-up before the assertion or the post-fix run is flaky-red at ~821 ms. With those three edits the test is exactly right: red today, green after.

Severity P1 stands. Not P0: prod traffic is effectively zero right now (16 requests/24h, CPU 0.0016 vCPU), so no user is being harmed today. Not P2: this is a hard serial ceiling on the single-worker single-loop deployment reachable by the first real user — one 3 MB PDP alone eats 2.1 s of the 15 s _PRICE_RACE_TIMEOUT and 7% of the 30 s STREAM_HARD_CAP while freezing /health, SSE heartbeats and auth for every concurrent request. The 18-wide fan-out model is supported by my corpus aggregate (sample n=62: parse p50 189.8 ms, mean 478.3 ms, p90 1388.8 ms) → 3.4 s (p50) to 8.6 s (mean) of hard loop block per cold compare, bracketing the finder's modelled 7.7 s.

Local env is off-lock per BRIEF rule 6, but this measurement is pure-Python CPU + asyncio scheduling with no framework introspection or SDK shape dependency, so the off-lock drift (fastapi/starlette/openai/pydantic/httpx/supabase) does not touch it; bs4/soupsieve are the only relevant deps and the parse cost is inherent to `html.parser`.

findings.title: The 40-thread pool is oversubscribed by ONE fragrance compare, not three: the speculative direct-adapter prefetch fires 32 sources per product = 64 concurrent to_thread work items before the escalation fan-out even starts
findings.dedupe: known:M18 LS-capacity-math-04 (P2, 'ThreadPoolExecutor-40 knee: 3rd concurrent cold fan-out queues') — still-open and UNDER-STATED: the input width it used (~18) is wrong at HEAD, the real width is 64 per compare, so the knee is C=1 and the severity is P1 not P2.
findings.fix: Two changes, both cheap. (a) Bound the prefetch: wrap the direct-adapter gathers at base structured_comparison_service.py:5871+ in an `asyncio.Semaphore(DIRECT_PREFETCH_CONCURRENCY, default 8)` created per compare, so the 32-per-product list drains in waves instead of all at once — this preserves the ranked ordering (highest-weight sources get threads first) and makes the per-source 10 s wrap meaningful again. (b) Re-derive the pool size from the measured width rather than the stale ~18: either raise ADAPTER_EXECUTOR_MAX_WORKERS (it is currently UNSET in prod, so 40) or, better, keep 40 and add the semaphore, because raising it trades thread starvation for the memory ceiling in finding 10. Also correct the docstring at executor.py:14-18 — it is now the load-bearing justification for a wrong number. Ship the semaphore behind ENABLE_PREFETCH_CONCURRENCY_CAP (default OFF, flag-OFF byte-identical).
findings.test_first: tests/test_prefetch_fanout_bound.py::test_direct_prefetch_never_exceeds_pool — monkeypatch each adapter's to_thread target to a counter that records max simultaneous in-flight, drive `_fetch_product_data` for a fragrance query with the catalog flag on, and assert max_in_flight <= default_executor_size(). Red today (it reaches 32 per product), green with the semaphore.
findings.impact: The knee is C=1, not the C=3 M18 modelled. A single cold fragrance compare submits >=64 work items against 40 workers, so ~24 of them sit in the pool's unbounded FIFO queue while a queued item's own `_timeout_none` 10 s wrap counts down. A queued adapter that never gets a thread returns None (finding 03) — i.e. the genuine-BHD source coverage the whole BH/GCC catalog build exists to deliver silently degrades by roughly a third at ZERO concurrency, and collapses entirely at C>=2 (128 work items / 40 workers, queue depth 88, every queued item exceeding its wrap). At C=10 the queue is ~600 deep and effectively nothing but the first 40 items returns. Because the losers are the LOW-priority tail of a pre-ordered list, the failure is biased toward the cheapest genuine sources, so the product falls back to converted_usd / GPT estimates exactly under load.

verdict_trail.reason: Repro reproduces EXACTLY once data/bh_gcc_sources.json is present (275 'live' rows): fragrances 32 = shopify 12 + gcc_shopify_pagescrape 6 + woo 6 + salla 2 + magento_gql 2 + algolia 1 + sitemap 1 + jsonapi 1 + noon 1; makeup 25, skincare 26, electronics 20, supplements 17, fashion 10 — every number matches. Live in prod (ENABLE_BH_GCC_CATALOG_SOURCES=true, ENABLE_PAGE_SCRAPE=true). Both products' _fetch_product_data run concurrently at scs:3327; prefetch gathers at 5866+. `grep -rn Semaphore app/` = 0 hits. Every adapter service reaches network via asyncio.to_thread (43 sites/20 files). M18 LS-capacity-math-04 (P2, '~18-24') is understated at HEAD; still-open.

Tried to break it and could not. I drove the REAL _get_price for two products concurrently (fragrances, catalog+page-scrape ON), instrumented asyncio.to_thread to occupy a real 40-worker qaren-worker pool, zero network. Measured 62 simultaneous submissions, 40 threads running, 21 items QUEUED at C=1 — the docstring's ~18/2-fan-outs is wrong. My first two runs showed a false 11 because the blocked Upstash retry (finding 04) stalled the loop 3 s per cache op; with Redis absent the burst is instantaneous. The semaphore fix closes it. test_first is right but must assert submitted-and-unfinished pool depth, not a naive in-flight counter, which loop stalls skew.

fable.note: Fable's P2 downgrade WITHDRAWN: measured 62 submissions / 21 queued against the real 40-worker pool from ONE fragrance compare

findings.title: Executor starvation is undetectable: _timeout_none drops every adapter to None with zero log lines and no counter, and the only other failure log in the fan-out is logger.debug under LOG_LEVEL=INFO
findings.dedupe: new — M18 LS-capacity-math-04 asserted the collapse is silent but did not identify the code that silences it, and no prior review noted the absence of a failure counter in fan_out_price_lookup's return contract.
findings.fix: Give the drop a name. In `_timeout_none`, split the handler: `except asyncio.TimeoutError: logger.info('[adapter] %s timed out after %.1fs', label, timeout); _ADAPTER_TIMEOUT_COUNT[label]+=1; return None` / `except Exception as e: logger.warning(...); return None`, threading a `label` argument from each of the ~12 call sites (they already know the family: sitemap/jsonapi/woo/salla/occ/magento_gql/unbxd/rest_json/noon/shopify_gcc). Add `failed_count` and `timed_out_count` to `fan_out_price_lookup`'s return dict alongside `cancelled_count`, surface both in the existing `_ps_mark` stage-timing block (DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS is already `true` in prod), and lift the two `logger.debug` fan-out lines to INFO. Unflagged — it is additive observability with no behaviour change, and it is a hard precondition for measuring any of the other fixes in this lane.
findings.test_first: tests/test_adapter_drop_observability.py::test_timeout_none_logs_and_counts — assert that `_timeout_none(slow_coro, 0.01, label='woo')` emits exactly one INFO record containing 'woo' and increments the family counter; and tests/test_fan_out_integration.py::test_fan_out_reports_failed_count — a fan-out where every scraper raises returns `failed_count == len(scrapers)`. Both red today.
findings.impact: This is the mechanism that makes findings 01/02/07 invisible in production. A compare in which every genuine-BH adapter timed out inside the executor queue produces exactly the same telemetry as a compare in which no Bahraini store carries the product: prices fall back to converted_usd/GPT estimate, the genuine-BH-share KPI silently drops, and nothing in Railway logs, Sentry or the admin cost meters records that a single thread-pool queue caused it. It also blocks any future load work: there is no way to tell from prod whether a capacity change helped, because the failure signal does not exist. The 690 'We don't compare this category' + 1288 'Still gathering prices' rows in search_logs are the only downstream trace and they attribute the outcome to the query, not to saturation.

verdict_trail.reason: Every factual claim reproduces: scs:212-230 is `except Exception: return None` with no logger/counter; the live repro printed `result=None records_after=1 timeout_mentions=0`. main.py:15 `configure_logging(os.getenv("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO"))` and LOG_LEVEL is absent from the 54 prod names, so the DEBUG lines at price_service 15898 / scs 1559 are dropped. fan_out_price_lookup returns cancelled_count only (15935-15940), no failed/timed_out. Downgraded because this is an absence of observability, not a defect users reach and not a launch gate: the user-visible degradation is findings 01/02. Also not 100% silent — scs 6045/6074/6108 log gather-level failures at INFO (per-source timeouts remain unlogged). Genuinely new.

findings.title: Every Upstash command runs on an httpx client with timeout=None and retries once through a blocking time.sleep(3) — on the single event loop, because ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD is unset in prod
findings.dedupe: known-adjacent:#71 (Redis/Supabase off the loop) — still-open. The unbounded timeout and the blocking 3 s retry sleep inside the vendor SDK are NOT in #71, M13 or M18; #71 is about moving the call off the loop, which does not remove the unbounded hang, it relocates it.
findings.fix: Two independent guards, both small. (a) Bound the socket: upstash-redis gives no timeout parameter, so construct the client and then replace its transport — after cache_service.py:28, `redis_client._http._client = httpx.Client(timeout=httpx.Timeout(UPSTASH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, connect=2.0))` (default 3.0 s, env-tunable), guarded in a try/except so an SDK-internal rename degrades to today's behaviour rather than crashing at import; pin the attribute path with a test so an upstash-redis bump cannot silently un-bound it. (b) Kill the blocking retry: pass `rest_retries=0` at construction, because a 3 s `time.sleep` on the event loop is never the right trade — the callers already fail-open (`_redis_get` returns None on any exception). Both are unflagged one-liners at a single site. Separately, this is the concrete argument for turning ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD on (#71): with it ON the sleep burns an executor thread instead of the loop — but note the pool is already oversubscribed per finding 02, so the offload must land after the semaphore.
findings.test_first: tests/test_cache_service_client.py::test_upstash_client_has_a_bounded_timeout — assert `redis_client._http._client.timeout.read is not None` and `<= 5.0`, and `redis_client._http._retries == 0`. Red today (timeout=None, retries=1).
findings.impact: Single loop, single worker, no timeout: one Upstash socket that accepts the connection and never answers freezes the ENTIRE deployment indefinitely — every in-flight compare, every SSE stream, /health included (main.py:307 is on the same loop). Railway's healthcheckPath is a deploy-time gate, not a liveness probe, so nothing restarts the worker; the outage is permanent until someone notices. The softer and far more likely case: any transient Upstash 5xx or connection reset triggers `time.sleep(3)` on the loop, so ONE failing cache read stalls all C concurrent requests for 3 s — and the request path makes on the order of 10-30 redis calls per compare (62 call sites across app/; the exact per-compare count is lane ls-cache-redis's to supply, I use 10-30 as a stated placeholder), so a degraded-but-not-down Upstash converts into minutes of frozen deployment. This is also why finding 01's loop budget cannot be reasoned about in isolation.

verdict_trail.reason: Verified against the LOCKED SDK, not the local off-lock one: downloaded upstash-redis==1.7.0 (requirements.txt:186) and read the wheel — `self._client = httpx.Client(timeout=None)`, `time.sleep(self._retry_interval)` in the retry loop, `rest_retries: int = 1`, `rest_retry_interval: float = 3`, and Redis.__init__ exposes no timeout parameter at all. cache_service.py:28 constructs with defaults only; _redis_get at 53 calls synchronously; ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD is absent from the 54 prod names so the offload is OFF and this runs on the single loop. Not reproduced against live Upstash (read-only rule + a hang cannot be induced) — that residual is honestly declared. #71 does not cover the unbounded timeout or the blocking retry. Correction: _redis_offload_enabled is at cache_service.py:539, not 549.

Reproduced live against local sockets, not by reading. A hanging endpoint left cache_service._redis_get blocked >25 s (timeout=None). A refused connection stalled the EVENT LOOP 7.08 s on ONE cache read. And in the real orchestrator run the 3 s retry serialized 66 adapter fetches to one per 3 s: 147.5 s vs 10.84 s with Redis absent — the deployment-freeze claim, measured. One correction: an HTTP 5xx does NOT retry (the SDK breaks on any response; only transport exceptions sleep), so 'any transient 5xx' is wrong. Locked 1.7.0 wheel matches 1.6.0. Fix (bounded transport + rest_retries=0) closes both limbs; test_first is fine but attribute-level — pin behaviour against a hanging socket instead.

fable.note: same defect as LS-REQUEST-PATH-BLOCKING-03

findings.title: Every httpx and Supabase client is built per call and each build parses the 136-cert certifi bundle on the event loop — measured 26.7 ms of CPU per construction, and run_db's offload cannot fix it because the construction sits outside the lambda
findings.dedupe: known:#73 (pooled httpx + bound GCC endpoint) — still-open. The SSL-context-per-construction cost, its measurement, the 40 Supabase per-call construction sites, and the 'the M24 offload does not cover it' corollary are new; #73 is scoped to connection reuse.
findings.fix: One shared SSL context and memoised clients. (a) Add `app/utils/ssl_context.py` with `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) def shared_ssl_context(): return httpx.create_ssl_context()`, and pass `verify=shared_ssl_context()` at all 20 `httpx.AsyncClient(...)` sites — that alone removes the cert parse without changing pooling semantics, and is far less risky than converting all 20 to long-lived pooled clients. (b) Memoise the Supabase factories: `auth_service.get_auth_client` and `get_admin_client` should use the same module-level singleton pattern database_service.py:44 already uses (they are stateless — the JWT is passed per call for the auth client). `get_user_supabase_client` genuinely needs per-token state via `client.postgrest.auth(token)`, so memoise the underlying client and set the token per call, or bound it with an LRU keyed on the token prefix. (c) Only then do the pooled-httpx work in #73. Ship (a) and (b) unflagged — they are construction-cost changes with identical request semantics — but land them BEFORE the M24 offload canary so that canary measures what it thinks it measures.
findings.test_first: tests/test_client_construction.py::test_supabase_auth_client_is_memoised — `assert get_auth_client() is get_auth_client()`; and ::test_httpx_clients_share_one_ssl_context — monkeypatch `ssl.SSLContext.load_verify_locations` with a counter, drive two serper searches through the real `search_web`, assert the counter did not increase. Both red today.
findings.impact: Pure CPU, on the single loop, with no I/O to hide behind. A cold compare constructs on the order of 15+ of these (serper discovery + shopping per product, exchange rate, firecrawl/scrapedo pairs, verify_token, save, usage) => >=15 x 26.7 ms ~ 400 ms of loop block per compare from certificate parsing ALONE, stacked on top of finding 01's ~7.7 s of parsing. On Railway (Linux, page-cached certifi) the disk half disappears but the 26.7 ms CPU half does not; the Railway number is UNMEASURED and the box here may be faster or slower than a Railway vCPU, so treat 15-30 ms as the honest per-construction range. The corollary matters more than the number: the planned M24 offload wave (#115/#116, ENABLE_SYNC_DB_OFFLOAD / ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD) will NOT remove this, because at auth_service.py:257 the expensive part is evaluated before `run_db` is called — so the wave will land, the graphs will barely move, and the cause will look mysterious.

verdict_trail.reason: The mechanism is real and reproduced. auth_service.py:30/37 build unmemoised clients; verify_token at 256-257 evaluates `client = get_auth_client()` OUTSIDE the run_db lambda, so the M24 offload cannot cover it — that corollary is correct and new. httpx 0.28.1 (locked wheel) create_ssl_context is still `ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=certifi.where())`, uncached. I measured the cert parse at 28.70 ms mean / 22.63 min over 136 certs (claim 26.72/23.60). Downgraded to P2: '>=15 constructions/compare ≈ 400 ms' is MODELLED (no live compare is possible), the Railway per-construction cost is admittedly unmeasured, and ~400 ms is ~5% of the finder's own finding-01 budget — a measurable cost issue, not a P1 defect. Minor count corrections: 19 httpx.AsyncClient sites (not 20), get_admin_client 13 call sites, get_user_supabase_client 19.

findings.title: The published Tier-1 OpenAI ceiling is ~32% too optimistic: measured verdict prompt is 5.5-5.8k tokens and OpenAI reserves the 1000-token max_tokens against TPM, giving ~4.4-4.6 verdicts/min, not 6.6 — below the 10/min limiter that is supposed to protect it
findings.dedupe: known:#117 / M18 LS-capacity-math-03 — still-open. The status is 'knobs shipped, none set in prod', and the fresh contribution is that the published arithmetic is wrong by ~32% in the unsafe direction, measured against recorded payloads through the real prompt builder.
findings.fix: Correct the runbook's §2 table to the measured 6.5-6.8k TPM/verdict and ~4.5/min, and state the reserved-max_tokens rule explicitly so the next person's arithmetic is right. Then take the cheapest lever, which the corrected number changes: dropping `max_tokens` on the verdict from 1000 to the observed completion size (the recorded verdicts are well under 700 tokens — measure them from the 27 stored `comparisons` rows first) buys back ~5% directly, but the real lever is the verdict cache the runbook already names — a cache keyed on the normalised product pair costs nothing and removes the binding call entirely for repeat pairs. Set OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES=1 and OPENAI_FALLBACK_MAX_RETRIES=0 in Railway as §3 instructs (they are currently unset; note the module-level client at openai_service.py:32 reads the knob at import, so this needs a restart). Do NOT change the limiter key (#114) until the corrected ceiling is above the limiter, not below it.
findings.test_first: tests/test_tpm_sizing.py::test_verdict_prompt_stays_within_the_budgeted_token_envelope — build the verdict prompt from the recorded fixtures and assert `prompt_tokens + VERDICT_MAX_TOKENS <= VERDICT_TPM_BUDGET_PER_CALL` (a named constant documented in the runbook), so a prompt-growth PR that silently lowers the throughput ceiling fails CI. Red the moment the constant is set to the runbook's current 4,500.
findings.impact: Three consequences. (1) The re-derived deployment-wide ceiling is ~4.4-4.6 compares/min at Tier 1, not 6.6-10 — which means the mis-keyed 10/min limiter bucket does NOT currently protect the OpenAI budget as the runbook's §2 'Interaction with #114' paragraph assumes; the front door already admits more than twice the OpenAI wall, so on the day credits are restored the FIRST sustained minute produces mid-compare 429s, not clean front-door 429s. (2) With both retry knobs unset the storm amplifies 3x on the primary and adds a second 3-attempt chain on mini, so effective throughput during saturation is ~1.5-2.3 verdicts/min — worse under load, which is the definition of a metastable failure. (3) Every downstream plan built on 6.6-10 (the #114 ordering rule, the M24 canary sizing) inherits the error. The account tier is UNVERIFIED; if it is Tier 2/3 the gpt-4o TPM rises to 450k/800k and this ceases to bind, but nothing in the repo records the tier and the runbook itself calls verification a hard gate.

verdict_trail.reason: The arithmetic error is real and I re-derived it independently through the real builder: prompt tokens 5564 / 5812 / 5942 across the three fixtures (finder: 5498/5614/5794) vs the runbook's ~4,500 at line 47. extraction_service.py:2447 passes `**token_limit_kwargs(verdict_model, 1000)` → `{'max_tokens': 1000}`, and verdict_chain_max_attempts()=6 with both retry envs unset (absent from the 54 prod names). Even discarding the ONE unverifiable premise — that OpenAI reserves max_tokens against TPM, which I cannot test (account is 429 insufficient_quota) — 30,000/5,800 = 5.2/min, still ~21% below the published 6.6. Downgraded to P2: this is a documentation-arithmetic defect with no code change and no user reach; no live compare is possible at all today, and the finder's own Tier-1 premise is unverified.

findings.title: Shopify domain-spacing reserves a slot and never releases it, so cancelled waiters permanently push the queue into the future: measured 60 s of 3 req/s leaves the storefront unreachable for 120 s AFTER load stops
findings.dedupe: new — not in M13, M18, the mobile checkup, or any of the 33 open issues.
findings.fix: Release the reservation on cancel and cap the queue. In `_await_domain_slot`, wrap the sleep: `wait = reserve_domain_slot(domain); if wait > MAX_DOMAIN_QUEUE_WAIT (default 2.0): release_domain_slot(domain); return False` — i.e. refuse the slot rather than queue behind an unreachable one, and add `release_domain_slot(key)` that rolls `_next_slot_at[key]` back by MIN_DOMAIN_INTERVAL_S, called both on the refusal path and from a `try/except asyncio.CancelledError` around the sleep. Callers already handle a miss (`return None, None`), so refusing early is strictly better than burning the 3 s budget. Also prune `_next_slot_at` of keys whose timestamp is in the past (it grows unbounded today). Ship behind ENABLE_DOMAIN_SLOT_RELEASE (default OFF, flag-OFF byte-identical) and canary it before any `--workers` change, since multi-worker makes the throttle wrong in the opposite direction and the correct multi-worker fix is a Redis-backed slot, not a module dict.
findings.test_first: tests/test_shopify_domain_spacing.py::test_cancelled_waiter_releases_its_slot — take 3 slots, cancel the 3rd waiter, assert the next caller's wait is 2.0 s not 3.0 s; and ::test_slot_queue_is_bounded — 20 simultaneous reservations, assert no returned wait exceeds MAX_DOMAIN_QUEUE_WAIT. Both red today.
findings.impact: Fragrances resolve to 12 Shopify storefronts (measured, finding 02) and a compare fetches BOTH products, so even C=1 puts 2 callers on each domain and C=2 puts 4 — at which point the 4th caller's 3.0 s wait exactly meets the wait_for and misses. Beyond that the failure is not transient: because cancelled callers keep their slots, a burst of C=3 sustained for a minute leaves the highest-value genuine-BHD storefronts unreachable for two further minutes with no traffic at all, and the loss is silent (`return None, None` at :301, then `_timeout_none` at finding 03). Shopify /products.json is the $0, zero-Serper, genuine-BHD price path — the exact source the BH/GCC catalog build exists to reach — so this converts a load spike into a persistent price-quality outage that looks like 'no Bahraini store carries this'. Under `--workers 2/4` it inverts: `_next_slot_at` is per-process module state, so N workers issue N requests per second per domain, i.e. the politeness guarantee the 12194-byte-503 incident motivated is silently multiplied by N.

verdict_trail.reason: Mechanics confirmed exactly: the repro returned [0.0..9.0] and 120.0. But reachability fails. Every network entry (fetch_shopify_pdp_json:525, fetch_ucp_json_product:866, _price:962, _availability:911) returns None unless ENABLE_SHOPIFY_PDP_JSON / ENABLE_UCP_JSON_PRICE is truthy; both default "false" and neither is among the 54 prod var names. The live Shopify /products.json path the impact section blames (price_service._fetch_shopify_catalog, and the 3s wait_for at scs:6421) never calls reserve_domain_slot — that attribution is wrong. Dark-flag latent defect, not a price-quality outage.

findings.title: Three to_thread adapters bypass adapter_timeout() and park executor threads 12-20 s behind a 3-10 s wrap — the exact defect M13-34 built adapter_timeouts.py to eliminate, adopted by 8 adapters and missed by the rest
findings.dedupe: known:M13-34 (adapter_timeouts.py landed) — partially-fixed/still-open: 8 of 12+ thread-holding adapters adopted the clamp, and the four listed here were never routed. Not itself an open issue.
findings.fix: Route the four thread-holding constants through the existing clamp: `HTTP_TIMEOUT = adapter_timeout(12)` (shopify_pdp_service.py:103), `_TIMEOUT = adapter_timeout(20)` (sitemap_discovery_service.py:390), `_TIMEOUT = adapter_timeout(12)` (yotpo_service.py:61), and `BH_REGISTRY_CURL_TIMEOUT = adapter_timeout(10)` (price_service.py:660) — each becomes 9.0 and none changes a returned result, only the moment the socket is abandoned, exactly as the module docstring argues. Shopify additionally deserves a tighter value than the shared ceiling because its own wrap is 3 s: `adapter_timeout(4)` keeps the thread inside the caller's budget. For the loop-bound render adapters, clamp FIRECRAWL_TIMEOUT and SCRAPEDO_TIMEOUT to the fan-out budget (`min(FIRECRAWL_TIMEOUT, _fan_out_budget_seconds())`) so a render call cannot be billed for work the race will discard. Unflagged — these are ceiling reductions on paths whose outer bound already fired.
findings.test_first: tests/test_adapter_timeouts.py::test_every_to_thread_adapter_is_clamped — walk the adapter modules with `ast`, collect module-level names matching `_?TIMEOUT` in files that contain `asyncio.to_thread`, and assert each resolved value `<= adapter_inner_ceiling()`. Red today on shopify_pdp (12), sitemap_discovery (20), yotpo (12) and price_service (10).
findings.impact: Multiplies finding 02. Shopify is the FIRST thing every escalation touches (12-18 domains per fragrance product), so on a cold or unresponsive store each source holds an executor thread for 12 s after its 3 s wait_for already gave up and returned None — 4x over-hold, on a pool that finding 02 shows is already oversubscribed by a single compare. Sitemap discovery holds 20 s against a 10 s wrap. The parked threads are invisible (the wrap already returned) and they are consumed by the NEXT compare's queue, so the damage lands on a different user than the one who caused it. adapter_timeouts.py has a test pinning `_ADAPTER_WRAP_TIMEOUT == scs._ADAPTER_TIMEOUT` so the two cannot drift, but nothing pins that every adapter actually uses the clamp — which is why the adoption stalled at 8.

verdict_trail.reason: adapter_inner_ceiling()=9.0 and the 8 adopters reproduce. Three of four named non-adopters are unreachable: shopify_pdp (dark flag, above), sitemap_discovery:390 is `_ROBOTS_TIMEOUT` (not `_TIMEOUT`), used only by the off-clock builder behind ENABLE_SITEMAP_INDEX and inside no adapter wrap, and yotpo_service has ZERO importers in app/ or tests/. The fourth is at 643 (not 660) at 76ace90, equals the 10.0 wrap rather than exceeding it, and its only live consumer is _lazy_bh_pdp_backfill, Serper-fired with SERPER_LIFETIME_LIMIT=0. No 12-20s park reproduced.

findings.title: The 40-thread pool has no memory bound: measured BeautifulSoup peak is 9.6x the HTML, the fan-out's own fetch has no max_bytes cap, and the corpus contains a 10.2 MB page — 40 concurrent p90 parses model to ~0.7 GB against a 0.136 GB idle RSS
findings.dedupe: new — M18 LS-capacity-math-05 (P3) flagged GIL contention and assumed a 3 MB cap that does not exist on this path; no prior review measured the BS4 expansion ratio or the corpus size distribution.
findings.fix: Cap the input before it becomes a tree. Add `max_bytes: int = 3_000_000` to `curl_fetch_html` (base price_service.py:13943) mirroring the same-site helper, truncating `resp.content` before `.text` — a PDP price never lives past 3 MB and the corpus max is a 10 MB outlier. Then, when finding 01's parse offload ships, bound the concurrent parse count separately from the fetch count (a dedicated `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=PARSE_POOL_SIZE, default 8)` for parses, distinct from the shared adapter pool) so that thread-count and memory-ceiling are tuned independently, and record the derivation in executor.py's docstring alongside the latency one. Do this in the SAME change as finding 01, never after it.
findings.test_first: tests/test_curl_fetch_bounds.py::test_curl_fetch_html_truncates_oversized_bodies — monkeypatch the to_thread target to return a 10 MB body and assert the returned html length is <= max_bytes. Red today (no cap exists).
findings.impact: MODELLED from the measured inputs: 40 simultaneous p90 parses peak at ~716 MB; at p99 (3.7 MB x ~9.6) ~1.4 GB; a single uncapped max-size page is ~100 MB in one thread. The idle RSS is 0.136 GB, so the container's headroom is entirely unmeasured against this — an OOM kill of the single worker is total downtime with `restartPolicyMaxRetries: 3` (railway.json:10-11) before permanent stop. This is the reason raising ADAPTER_EXECUTOR_MAX_WORKERS is NOT the right answer to finding 02: more workers trades thread starvation for an OOM. Note the parses currently happen on the LOOP (finding 01), so today the concurrency is 1 and memory is safe by accident — moving them into the pool without a size cap is what makes this live.

verdict_trail.reason: Inputs reproduce exactly — 1,235 files, p50 376,925 / p90 1,725,944 / p99 3,714,881 / max 10,484,487 B, and BS4 peaks of 2.35x-11.76x bracket the claimed 9.6x; 40 x 17.85 MB = 714 MB checks out. executor.py:30 and the missing max_bytes on curl_fetch_html are real. But the finder concedes the parses run on the loop today (concurrency 1), and the uncapped helper's only live caller does `re.findall`, not BS4; every BS4-fed fetch goes through curl_fetch_html_same_site, which IS capped at 3_000_000. No live memory exposure.

findings.title: No backpressure at the ASGI front door: uvicorn runs with no --limit-concurrency, so under overload the single loop queues without bound instead of shedding with 503 — the cheapest unfiled lever
findings.dedupe: new for --limit-concurrency. known:M18 LS-event-loop-07 (--workers, P2) still-open and LS-railway-metrics-04 (memory:// multi-worker semantics) still-open — both are folded into the fix's ordering rather than re-found.
findings.fix: Set the start command in railway.json:7 and Procfile:1 to `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT --limit-concurrency ${UVICORN_LIMIT_CONCURRENCY:-40} --timeout-keep-alive 15 --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*'`, choosing the limit from the corrected ceilings in this lane (the binding one today is finding 01's ~7.8 compares/min, so 40 in-flight is generous and only sheds real overload). Note `--proxy-headers` is a SEPARATE decision that interacts with #114 — do not add it in the same change, because it changes what `get_remote_address` returns and therefore the limiter key that currently protects the loop. On `--workers 2/4`: it buys N loops (a real N-fold lift on findings 01/05, which are the binding ones) and N x the RSS, but it BREAKS four things — slowapi's `memory://` bucket becomes per-process so every rate limit silently multiplies by N (rate_limiter.py:103-110); shopify's `_next_slot_at` politeness throttle multiplies by N (finding 07); the per-process observability counters (`_SHOPPING_PRIMARY_SKIPPED_COUNT`, `_CACHE_READ_REJECTED_COUNT`, `_varhint_calls_this_run`) under-report by 1/N and feed the admin meters (#66); and the 40-thread pool becomes 40N threads on the same container CPU. The Redis-backed budget/breaker state in api_budget_service survives multi-worker correctly. So the honest ordering is: --limit-concurrency first (free, safe), then findings 01/05, then --workers only after the limiter storage moves off memory://.
findings.test_first: tests/test_start_command.py::test_start_command_declares_a_concurrency_limit — parse railway.json and Procfile and assert both contain `--limit-concurrency` and that the two commands are byte-identical to each other (they can drift today and nothing notices). Red now.
findings.impact: Combine with findings 01/04: the loop is blocked for ~7.7 s per cold compare from parsing and can be blocked indefinitely by one Upstash socket. With no concurrency limit, arriving requests are accepted and queued rather than rejected, so latency degrades without bound and every waiting client's own 120 s mobile timeout fires — the app then retries (mobile falls back SSE->REST), which adds load at exactly the wrong moment. That is the metastable-collapse shape: the system never recovers on its own even after the offered load returns to normal. A 503 at the door is strictly better than a 120 s spinner, and it is the ONE lever that costs nothing, needs no code, and is instantly reversible. M18 filed `--workers 2` (LS-event-loop-07) as the cheap lever but not this one; adding workers without a concurrency limit multiplies the queue, it does not bound it.

verdict_trail.reason: Every claim holds at HEAD. railway.json:7 and Procfile:1 carry the bare uvicorn command; grep for limit-concurrency/limit_concurrency/backlog/timeout-keep-alive/workers over both returns nothing (exit 2), and no nixpacks.toml overrides it. _get_storage_uri returns memory:// unconditionally, and the blanket default_limits are gated at main.py:137 on a flag absent from the 54 prod names — so admission control today is one deployment-wide in-process bucket with no ASGI backpressure. Genuinely new: 'limit-concurrency' appears 0 times in the M18 verified set. Held at P2, not P1: prospective, never load-tested, prod traffic is ~0.

findings.title: Every activation precondition in the #117 launch runbook is unset in prod and nothing detects it: 6 flags absent, verdict_chain_max_attempts()=6, and STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS is 30 while every code comment and the M18 arithmetic assume 25
findings.dedupe: known:#117 — status still-open (knobs shipped, none applied). The STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS 25-vs-30 code/prod divergence and the absence of any config-observability surface are fresh; M18 recorded the flags as 'shipped', not as 'shipped and unset with no way to tell'.
findings.fix: Make the resolved configuration observable, then set it. Add a single startup log line in the existing `@app.on_event("startup")` handler (main.py:168) — a one-line JSON dump of `{executor_size, verdict_chain_max_attempts, stream_hard_cap, price_race_timeout, fan_out_budget, sync_db_offload, async_redis_offload, full_stream_deadline, preverdict_abort, proxy_aware_ratelimit, resolved_models}` using the helpers that already exist (`default_executor_size`, `verdict_chain_max_attempts`, `resolved_models`) — so 'what is actually running' is one grep away instead of a 54-name variable audit. Expose the same dict on an admin-keyed `GET /api/v1/admin/config` next to the existing cap gauges. Then set OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES=1 and OPENAI_FALLBACK_MAX_RETRIES=0 as §3 instructs, and pair ENABLE_FULL_STREAM_DEADLINE=true with re-funding as §4 calls a HARD pairing. Separately: reconcile STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS — either drop the prod override to 25 or update base scs:1365's default and the four comments to 30; leaving code and prod disagreeing is how the M18 latency numbers went stale.
findings.test_first: tests/test_startup_config_report.py::test_startup_logs_resolved_concurrency_config — run the startup handler with caplog and assert the emitted record contains every key above with a non-None value; plus tests/test_stream_cap_comments.py::test_stream_cap_default_matches_its_docstring — grep base scs for 'STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS=' in comments and assert the literal equals the module default. Both red today.
findings.impact: The runbook reads as a checklist that has been completed — the knobs shipped, the arithmetic is written down, #117 is closed — but nothing it prescribes is actually in effect, and there is no way to tell from the running deployment. When credits are restored, the verdict chain will burn 6 upstream attempts per verdict into a budget that finding 06 shows is already ~2x oversubscribed by the front door, and the SSE tail will run OUTSIDE the cap (ENABLE_FULL_STREAM_DEADLINE off) so a single degraded call can hold a connection for minutes on the one worker. The STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS drift is the same class of hazard in miniature: prod runs 30 while four in-code comments and the M18 latency model reason about 25, so the data-fetch stage alone may consume 30 s before the verdict tail begins. `git log` shows nobody re-derived the comments when the variable was set.

verdict_trail.reason: All ten env names are absent from the 54 prod names; verdict_chain_max_attempts() returns 6 on a clean env at model_config.py:205 exactly as cited. STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS defaults to 25.0 at scs:1365 while Railway sets 30 — a live code/prod divergence. The observability gap is real: startup does only install_default_executor and /health returns status+message. Two corrections: the second comment is at scs:5067, not 5148, and there are two such comments in-code, not four. M18 knew prod was 30 but never flagged the divergence or the missing config surface.

findings.title: ENABLE_TPM_AWARE_ROUTING is listed in CLAUDE.md's Feature Flags as a shipped knob but has zero implementation — setting it in Railway silently does nothing
findings.dedupe: new — not in M13, M18, the mobile checkup, or the 33 open issues; #117 is closed and its own runbook correctly records the deferral, so the defect is purely that CLAUDE.md contradicts it.
findings.fix: Either implement it or stop advertising it. The cheap correct move now is to move the CLAUDE.md:394 entry out of the Feature Flags list into a clearly-labelled 'Planned / NOT implemented' subsection with a one-line pointer to runbook §5, so the flag index only lists flags that exist. If it is to be built, the runbook already specifies it correctly: a per-minute Redis window on the atomic INCRBY idiom that `tests/test_model_router.py::test_record_usage_uses_atomic_incrby` pins, downshifting `get_model('high')` to the standard model when the minute's projected tokens exceed a threshold derived from the VERIFIED tier — and note that `_get_4o_usage_today`/`_increment_4o_usage` (model_router_service.py:89, :107) call `_redis_get`/`redis_client.incrby` synchronously from `async def`, so a per-minute check adds two more blocking Upstash round-trips per verdict on the loop unless it lands after finding 04.
findings.test_first: tests/test_flag_inventory.py::test_every_documented_flag_is_read_by_code — parse the `ENABLE_*` names out of CLAUDE.md's Feature Flags section and assert each appears in an `os.getenv`/`os.environ` call under app/. Red today on ENABLE_TPM_AWARE_ROUTING, and it would have caught this class of drift at authoring time.
findings.impact: CLAUDE.md's flag list is the operator's index of what can be turned on, and this entry sits among real flags with a real issue number and a real-sounding description. An operator restoring OpenAI credits under time pressure — exactly the scenario the runbook is written for — would reasonably set ENABLE_TPM_AWARE_ROUTING=true, get no error, no log, no behaviour change, and believe the TPM wall from finding 06 is now guarded when it is not. The daily counter it claims to supplement is structurally incapable of firing before a mid-minute TPM wall (it needs 800,000 gpt-4o tokens in a day to trip; at the measured 6.6k tokens/verdict that is ~120 verdicts, roughly 27 minutes of sustained traffic — long after the per-minute wall). This is the same class as the two live breakages fixed 2026-09-02: documentation asserting a capability the wire does not have.

verdict_trail.reason: Every factual claim reproduces: CLAUDE.md:394 is exactly the ENABLE_TPM_AWARE_ROUTING bullet, sitting between real flags in the Feature Flags list; `grep -rn ENABLE_TPM_AWARE_ROUTING app/` returns zero; model_router_service.py is 114 lines with only DAILY_4O_CAP=1_000_000 (:37) and SWITCH_THRESHOLD=0.80 (:41) against a UTC-daily key, no per-minute window; the runbook's own section 5 records the deferral. Downgraded to P3 because the defect is documentation-only — no code path, no data, no spend moves. It misleads an operator; it breaks nothing.

findings.title: The #117 retry ceiling misses the fifth AsyncOpenAI construction: url_extraction_service builds its client without max_retries, so /url/extract and /url/compare keep 3 attempts per call whatever OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES says
findings.dedupe: known:#117 — the issue is closed; this is an incomplete-fix gap, not a re-find. New.
findings.fix: Add `max_retries=openai_max_retries()` to url_extraction_service.py:31, importing the helper the same way extraction_service.py:48 does (a local import inside `get_client` to keep the module's import graph unchanged). Default 2 == the SDK default, so this is byte-identical until the env is set — the change is that the knob then actually reaches the path. Correct the runbook §3 table to say 'all five AsyncOpenAI constructions' and list them.
findings.test_first: tests/test_openai_retry_knob.py::test_every_async_openai_construction_honours_the_knob — set OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES=1, reset each module's memo, and assert `client.max_retries == 1` for all five constructions (openai_service.client requires a module reload since it reads at import — assert that explicitly so the restart requirement is pinned rather than folklore). Red today on url_extraction_service.
findings.impact: Small but real, and it is a correctness gap in a bound that exists precisely to be exact. During a 429 storm the URL path's two per-compare extraction calls each retry 3x regardless of the launch setting, adding ~4,800 reserved tokens per URL compare into an already-saturated mini budget at the moment the knob was set to prevent exactly that. It also means `model_config.verdict_chain_max_attempts()` — documented as 'the EXPLICIT worst-case upstream attempt count' — does not describe the URL path at all. Note the URL compare route is separately unmetered per the mobile checkup lead, so it is not rate-limited into safety either.

verdict_trail.reason: Reproduced at 76ace90 (files byte-identical to working tree). Five AsyncOpenAI constructions exist; only url_extraction_service:31 lacks max_retries, and runbook line 75 literally says 'all four'. Reachable unauthed via POST/GET /url/extract and /url/compare (limiter 10/min), through extract_from_url:450 -> extract_with_ai -> get_client:385, twice per compare via asyncio.gather:537. Arithmetic checks: 800 tok x 2 calls x 3 attempts = 4,800. OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES is absent from prod vars, so today it is byte-identical to the SDK default 2 — latent, P3 correct. Fix is flag-safe. New (url_extraction_service absent from M18 rows).

findings.title: P3 sweep: five smaller concurrency defects found while walking the surface
findings.dedupe: new for (a)-(e) as stated; (a) is adjacent to known:#68 (fire-and-forget failures -> Sentry, still-open) which covers the logging, not the boundedness.
findings.fix: (a) Route `fire_and_forget` through a module-level `asyncio.Semaphore(BACKGROUND_TASK_CONCURRENCY, default 16)` and add a gauge of in-flight background tasks to the existing stage-timing block, so background work becomes visible and bounded; keep the done-callback logging (#68 wants it in Sentry). (b) Add an `@app.on_event("shutdown")` that calls `executor.shutdown(wait=True, cancel_futures=True)` on the executor returned by `install_default_executor` (store it on `app.state`) and closes the memoised clients. (c) Note the anyio pool in executor.py's docstring and, if any sync dependency ever grows real work, set `anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter().total_tokens` explicitly at startup. (d) Prune `_next_slot_at` in finding 07's change.
